beats.narration_text: Hello, I'm Vineet S.. You do not need to train a language model to manage a product built on one. But you do need a mental model of how it behaves. Here are the seven ideas that matter most.

props.segment: How AI Product Managers Work with LLMs
props.command: What does a product manager need to know about LLMs?

beats.narration_text: A language model is a predictor that writes the most likely text. It does not look facts up. That one idea explains why it can sound confident and still be wrong, and why a product manager's job is to design around it.

props.text:
A language model
is a database that
looks up the right answer.
props.triggerWords: a database that, looks up the right answer
props.replacementWords: a predictor that, writes the most likely text

beats.narration_text: Here are the seven ideas. Prompts. The context window. Tokens. Hallucinations. Fine-tuning. Retrieval, or R A G. And A P Is. Each one is a lever or a risk, and each one changes what you can promise users.

props.caption: Each is a lever or a risk

beats.narration_text: Start with the inputs. The prompt is the instruction, and small wording changes can change the output a lot. The context window is how much text the model can consider at once, so long documents may not fit. Tokens are the pieces of words that text is split into, and cost and speed are usually counted in tokens.

layers.title: Prompt
layers.sub: Instructions and examples you give the model

layers.title: Context window
layers.sub: How much text it can consider at once

layers.title: Tokens
layers.sub: Pieces of words; cost and speed count them

beats.narration_text: Now the big risk. A hallucination is a fluent answer that is not true. The model blends patterns, style and what it remembers, and the result sounds just as confident whether it is right or wrong. For example, it may cite a source that does not exist. A product manager plans for this with checks, citations, and a way for users to verify.

props.arcCaption: For example: a source that does not exist

beats.narration_text: When answers are not good enough, there is a ladder. Try better prompts first, because they are cheapest. If the model lacks your facts, use retrieval, which hands it your documents at answer time. If it needs a different style or skill, consider fine-tuning, which trains it further on examples. Pick the lightest fix that works.

layers.title: Retrieval (RAG)
layers.sub: Give it your documents at answer time

layers.title: Fine-tuning
layers.sub: Train on examples to change style or skill

beats.narration_text: Most teams reach a model through an A P I. That makes the model a dependency. You pay per use, the provider may change or retire the model, privacy terms matter, there are rate limits, and you need a fallback for when it is down. Treat it like any critical vendor.

props.caption: Treat it like a critical vendor

beats.narration_text: So what does the product manager actually do? Define good with test cases before launch. Design for wrong answers, with citations, review, and an undo. Watch cost and speed, because tokens add up. And keep a human in the loop wherever the stakes are high.
So, working with language models. They predict likely text. Know the seven ideas. Plan for hallucinations. Choose the lightest fix. And keep a human where it matters.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Paste this into Claude. I am a product manager planning an AI feature that uses a language model: [describe it]. Explain which of prompts, context window, tokens, hallucinations, fine-tuning, RAG and API choices matter most for it, give me the top three risks in plain language, and suggest one test I can run this week. Then tell me what I am probably overestimating about the model. The last sentence is the useful one. Overconfidence about the model is the most common planning error, so look at what Claude says you are overestimating, and test that first. Pause here and run it on your own product.
